source.title: Comparative Generalization Bounds for Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Tomer Galanti; Liane Galanti; Ido Ben-Shaul

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own results on effective depth, partially corrupted labels, and test error, using NCC separability and a derived bound rather than the interventions or measures named in the claim versions. Its reported outcomes do not test any version as specifically stated.
record.gate_note: The study reports corrupted-label effects on intermediate-layer NCC separability and estimates of test error and a generalization bound. It does not report the train-versus-test error gap or compare the specific conditions in V1–V8. Cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study measures effective depth, intermediate-layer NCC separability, and generalization bounds. Its own results do not establish any V1–V8 comparison. Partially corrupted labels do not establish V1's coexistence of near-perfect fully random-label fitting and natural-label generalization; depth sweeps do not test V2's width claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that sufficiently deep, successfully trained networks tend to converge to similar effective depths within a tested setting, and that comparing effective depth with the minimal NCC depth needed for partially corrupted labels provides useful empirical predictions of test performance. Their reported non-vacuous bound estimates use approximations and assumptions about negligible remainder terms.
record.recipe_differences: Measures NCC separability and proposes a bound based on effective depth and partially corrupted labels; it does not apply the original studies' interventions or measures in V1–V8.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, architecture, corrupted-label fraction, and epsilon affect the reported effective-depth measurements.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 4.2 reports effective depth 5 without corruption and 6 with at least 25% corruption at epsilon 0.02, subject to the source inconsistencies noted for R2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing partial label corruption can reduce intermediate-layer NCC separability and increase effective depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 2 reports mean test errors of 0.0075, 0.0996, 0.2676, and 0.29 across four architecture–dataset combinations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: These trained classifiers achieve the reported held-out errors under the study's SGD recipe; these errors alone do not validate the proposed bound.

record.problems: The paper notes that its uniform-mistake and corrupted-label depth assumptions may be violated in practice. Its empirical estimates use limited splits and initializations; the bound estimation assumes two terms are negligible and uses an approximation to minimal depth. The reported results do not provide paired train and test error for the claim's generalization-gap outcome.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure-only layer-by-layer measurements were not transcribed because the text does not give their precise values; the explicit textual comparison in Section 4.2 is recorded in R1–R2.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fully random labels, natural-label held-out performance under the same recipe, and chance held-out performance with fully random labels are not jointly tested. Corruption experiments use partial corruption and explicit weight decay.
No width sweep beyond the width required for zero training error; the reported sweeps vary depth.

No established comparison of convolutional versus fully connected test error, or intervention on learned local connectivity or convolutional initialization. Both architecture types appear in NCC analyses.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison or tuning comparison.
No batch-size comparison; batch size is fixed at 128.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or ranking of generalization gaps. Comparing norm-based bounds with an effective-depth bound does not test this version.
No removal of examples selected by memorization influence, retraining, or random-removal control.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels apply. The study cites V1's original finding as background and investigates a different explanation of generalization. Missing paired training errors are not the general reason for exclusion: the decisive issue is the absence of the specific comparisons named by V1–V8. Figure curves cannot be reconstructed from the supplied text's axes and legends.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test fitting fixed random labels alongside natural labels and comparing held-out accuracy.
Does not sweep width across the interpolation threshold or report test error as a function of width.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected networks on the same image tasks as specified.
Uses SGD, but does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD.
Does not vary batch size or compare large- and small-batch training.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with other gap measures.
Does not remove memorized examples and retrain.

rows.subject: CONV-10-400
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR10 with 0% corrupted labels; measured effective depth using NCC train error.
rows.locator: Section 4.2, NCC separability with partially corrupted labels
rows.note: The paper contrasts this with training using at least 25% corrupted labels.
rows.check: The reported effective depth of 5 matches Section 4.2, but effective depth alone cannot determine any claim version's effect.

rows.subject: CONV-10-400
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR10 with at least 25% corrupted labels; measured effective depth using NCC train error.
rows.locator: Section 4.2, NCC separability with partially corrupted labels
rows.note: The text also states the sixth layer's NCC accuracy drops below 98% for this condition, versus above 98% without corrupted labels.
rows.check: The reported depth of 6 matches the authors' statement, but measures no claim version. The source is internally inconsistent: its setup lists 10% corruption while Figure 3 shows 25%, and sixth-layer accuracy below 98% conflicts with effective depth 6 at epsilon 0.02. Preserve these as source ambiguities.
